spatial_claims.claim: B, G, F are three distinct points lying on both circle 1 and circle 2 (assumed for contradiction)
Circle 1 and circle 2 cut one another (intersect)
K is the center of circle 1
B, G, F lie on the circumference of circle 1, so KB = KG = KF (equal radii)
B, G, F lie on circle 2, so three equal lines from K fall upon circle 2
Three equal lines from interior point K to circle 2 implies K is center of circle 2 (by 3.9)
Circles 1 and 2 share center K but cut each other, contradicting 3.5
From external point K, at most two equal lines can fall on circle 2 (by 3.8), but three do
Case 3: K lies on the circumference of circle 2
K is on the diameter of circle 2 through K (as an endpoint) and is not the center of circle 2
From point K on diameter of circle 2, not the center, at most two equal lines fall on circle 2 (by 3.7), but three do

configuration_map: Configuration: Two circles (circle 1 and circle 2) that cut each other, assumed to intersect at three distinct points B, G, F. K is the center of circle 1, so KB = KG = KF. The position of K relative to circle 2 is unknown and handled by exhaustive case analysis: (1) K inside circle 2, (2) K outside circle 2, (3) K on circle 2. In each case, the three equal segments from K to points on circle 2 yield a contradiction via propositions 3.9, 3.8, and 3.7 respectively. No auxiliary constructions create conflicting spatial claims. The only construction beyond the initial setup is drawing a diameter of circle 2 through K in Case 3.
pass_reason: The proof uses a clean exhaustive case analysis on K's position relative to circle 2 (inside, outside, on circumference). Each case correctly applies the corresponding proposition (3.9, 3.8, 3.7) to derive a contradiction from three equal lines falling from K to circle 2. No angle decompositions, ray-ordering claims, or betweenness claims are made. All spatial claims are mutually consistent within each case, and the three cases are exhaustive. The proof contains no spatial configuration contradictions.
